title: Samut Songkhram–Phetchaburi 3-Day Trip, Thailand
metaDesc: A 3-day Samut Songkhram–Phetchaburi route in Thailand: Maeklong Railway Market, Amphawa Floating Market, firefly boats, then Khao Wang and custard cake — with hours, prices, and directions.
keywords: Samut Songkhram Phetchaburi trip, cross-province itinerary Thailand, Amphawa Floating Market Khao Wang, Maeklong Phetchaburi 3 days, Phetchaburi old town custard cake
intro: These two provinces sit only about 40 minutes apart, but they feel completely different. Samut Songkhram is all floating markets, the railway market, and quiet evening canals, while Phetchaburi is an old town with a palace on a hill, ancient temples, and sweets that have been made the same way for a hundred years. This plan links the two over 3 days and 2 nights — you're at the first stop just an hour out of Bangkok, then you work your way south without ever backtracking.

blocks.html: If you've got a long three-day weekend and want both the buzz of a floating market and the calm of an old town in one trip, the Samut Songkhram–Phetchaburi route fits the bill nicely. The two provinces line up along the same road — driving from Amphawa down to Phetchaburi takes only about 40–50 minutes — so there's no looping around or doubling back.

The heart of this plan is simple: spend the first two days in Samut Songkhram hitting the railway market, the floating market, and a firefly boat ride, then cross into Phetchaburi on day three to walk the old town, visit the temples, and grab custard cake to take home. To make it line up perfectly, aim to leave on a Friday — Amphawa Floating Market only runs Friday to Sunday, and those are the nights you can ride out to watch the fireflies.

From Bangkok, take Rama II Road (Highway 35) down to Maeklong town, roughly 70 kilometres, which is a little over an hour. After that, everything in Samut Songkhram is close together — most stops are only a few minutes' drive apart. Once day two wraps up, you carry on from Amphawa on Highway 4 (Phetkasem) into Phetchaburi town, about 45 kilometres, under an hour.

items: Driving yourself — easily the most convenient option for this trip, since a few spots like Khao Luang Cave and Bang Kung Camp are hard to reach by public transport.

No car — you can take a Bangkok–Maeklong van from the Southern Bus Terminal (Sai Tai Mai), then get around town by songthaew or motorbike taxi. For the leg over to Phetchaburi, there are regular Maeklong–Phetchaburi vans.

The Maeklong railway line — if you're after the experience, try the Wongwian Yai–Mahachai train, cross the river by ferry, then catch the Ban Laem–Maeklong service. Only a few trains run each day, so check the times before you go.

blocks.title: Line your days up with the markets
blocks.html: Amphawa Floating Market only opens Friday to Sunday, roughly 11:00–20:00. The Maeklong Railway Market runs every day, but weekends are far busier. If you plan the trip for Friday to Sunday, you'll catch the floating market, the railway market, and the firefly boat all in one go.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Maeklong, the railway market, and riverside temples

blocks.html: Day one is about ticking off the highlights in Maeklong town. Start with the railway market — the image most people picture when they think of this province — then visit a couple of old riverside temples before settling into your accommodation around Amphawa.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: From the umbrella-pulldown market to the Maeklong riverside

items.activity: Leave Bangkok via Rama II; grab breakfast somewhere along the way
items.note: You'll reach Maeklong town around 10:00.

items.activity: Maeklong Railway Market (Talad Rom Hub) — watch the vendors pull in their awnings as the train comes through
items.note: Trains pass through about 4 times a day; check the schedule with the vendors in the market — there's usually a late-morning run around 11:00.

items.activity: Lunch at a riverside restaurant in Maeklong — try the local short-bodied mackerel and river prawns
items.note: Maeklong's stubby, bent-faced mackerel is the province's signature catch.

items.activity: Wat Phet Samut Worawihan — pay respects to Luang Pho Ban Laem, a revered temple in the middle of town
items.note: Open daily, free entry; locals in Maeklong hold this temple in high regard.

items.activity: Wat Chulamani — see the handsome teak ordination hall and pay respects to Luang Pho Nueang
items.note: An old Ayutthaya-era temple popular with people who come to ask for blessings.

items.activity: Check in around Amphawa and rest up before dinner
items.note: A canalside homestay gives you the best atmosphere.

items.activity: Eat your way through Amphawa Floating Market in the evening — noodles, fried snacks, sweets
items.note: On Friday-to-Sunday nights the floating market is at its liveliest.

items.activity: Take an evening firefly boat along the lamphu trees lining the canal
items.note: Boats leave from around 19:00, roughly 60–80 THB per person; the fireflies show up best on a moonless night.

blocks.title: About the railway market
blocks.html: What makes Talad Rom Hub special is the split second the train rolls in and the vendors pull back their awnings and goods all at once. For a good photo, get into position about 15 minutes before the train arrives, pick an angle that doesn't block the tracks, and keep an eye on your belongings when it gets crowded. The train times can change, so ask a vendor on the spot rather than trusting an old timetable.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Amphawa, the Rama II Memorial Park, and Bang Kung Camp

blocks.html: Day two stays around Amphawa the whole time. Ease into it by walking the Thai houses at the Rama II Memorial Park, which sits right next to the floating market, then move on to Bang Kung Camp to see the temple wrapped entirely in tree roots, before coming back to spend another night around Amphawa.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Rama II's Thai houses and the bodhi-wrapped temple

items.activity: Breakfast at a canalside café in Amphawa
items.note: This area has several riverside cafés that open early.

items.activity: King Rama II Memorial Park — walk among the cluster of Thai houses and the museum of early Rattanakosin-era objects
items.note: Open 08:30–16:30, closed Wednesdays; entry roughly 40 THB for adults, 60 THB for foreigners.

items.activity: Stroll the garden of plants from classical literature and the central-Thai house photo spots
items.note: A shady spot, with trees that appear in poetry from the reign of Rama II.

items.activity: Lunch by the Amphawa canal — try boat noodles and grilled prawns
items.note: Midday is less crowded, so it's an easier walk than in the evening.

items.activity: Bang Kung Camp + the bodhi-wrapped temple — pay respects to Luang Pho Nin Mani in the hall completely encased in tree roots
items.note: The temple is open 08:00–16:30; it's an iconic image of the province, and the late-afternoon light photographs well.

items.activity: See the boxer statues and the old camp walls, and wander beneath the big trees
items.note: Inside the camp there's a wide, shady open area — a cool, easy walk.

items.activity: Head back to your accommodation around Amphawa and relax
items.note: Save your energy tonight for Phetchaburi tomorrow.

items.activity: Dinner by the canal — try Amphawa sweets like coconut sticky rice and old-style Thai desserts
items.note: If you didn't get your fill at the floating market yesterday, you can do another round tonight.

blocks.title: About Bang Kung Camp
blocks.html: The bodhi-wrapped temple is the top photo spot — the roots of four large trees (bodhi, banyan, krai, and krang) creep over the building until you can barely see the walls. Morning or late-afternoon light gives better photos than the harsh sun at midday. Inside sits Luang Pho Nin Mani, an old stucco Buddha image that people in the area hold dear.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Crossing over to old-town Phetchaburi

blocks.html: On the last morning, check out and drive south to Phetchaburi — about 45 kilometres on Highway 4, reaching town in under an hour. Phetchaburi is an old town with a palace on a hill, ancient temples, a cave where light filters down onto a Buddha image, and sweets that have been passed down through several generations. Today is built to cover the temples and the food before you head home.

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Khao Wang, ancient temples, and custard cake

items.activity: Check out of Amphawa and drive down to Phetchaburi via Phetkasem
items.note: About 45 kilometres; you'll reach town around 09:30.

items.activity: Phra Nakhon Khiri (Khao Wang) — take the cable car up to the Rama IV palace on the hilltop and the viewpoint over Phetchaburi town
items.note: Open 08:30–16:30; museum entry roughly 20 THB for adults, 150 THB for foreigners; the cable car up and down is about 80 THB.

items.activity: Wat Mahathat Worawihan — see the white five-spired prang in the centre of town
items.note: Phetchaburi's landmark temple; open daily, free entry, and a popular photo spot.

items.activity: Lunch in the old town — try Phetchaburi-style khao chae or the local chilli-sauce noodles
items.note: Khao chae is easy to find in the hot season; it's the town's go-to dish for beating the heat.

items.activity: Wat Yai Suwannaram — see the murals and the Ayutthaya-era teak sermon hall
items.note: An old temple where you can see Phetchaburi craftsmanship up close; free entry.

items.activity: Khao Luang Cave — head down to pay respects to the Buddha images, with sunlight filtering through an opening in the ceiling onto the statues
items.note: The light filters down most beautifully in the late morning to early afternoon; there are lots of monkeys, so watch what's in your hands.

items.activity: Stop to buy custard cake and souvenirs before heading back
items.note: Old-name shops like Mae Kim Lai and Mae Kim Lang have several branches, both in town and along Phetkasem.

items.activity: Set off back to Bangkok
items.note: The drive home via Phetkasem–Rama II takes about two and a half hours.

blocks.title: About Khao Wang
blocks.html: Khao Wang has two ways up — climb the fairly steep stone staircase, or take the electric cable car, which is far easier, especially on a sunny day. At the top there's the palace, the Phra That Chom Phet stupa, and temples you can walk between. Monkeys are all over the place, so don't carry food bags out in the open, and keep an eye on your glasses and hat.

blocks.text: Food in both towns you shouldn't miss

blocks.html: You'll eat well in both provinces on this trip. Samut Songkhram shines for its seafood and canalside sweets, while Phetchaburi is a genuine town of sweets. Here's what to try before you head home.

items.name: Maeklong mackerel
items.blurb: Short-bodied, bent-faced mackerel — rich, sweet meat, steamed in traditional bamboo baskets. A signature dish worth trying on your first day in Maeklong.

items.name: Amphawa canalside sweets
items.blurb: Coconut sticky rice, old-style Thai desserts, and riverside coffee. Graze your way along in the evening for the full floating-market atmosphere.

items.name: Phetchaburi custard cake
items.blurb: Custard cake with a caramelised top and the scent of pandan; old-name shops like Mae Kim Lai and Mae Kim Lang have been making it for decades. A great souvenir to bring home.

items.name: Phetchaburi khao chae
items.blurb: Rice in flower-scented chilled water, eaten with fried and sweet-savoury side dishes — the town's classic dish for beating the heat, easy to find in the hot season.

items: Pick Friday to Sunday if you want both Amphawa Floating Market and the firefly boat — the market only opens on these three days.
Book ahead — canalside homestays in Amphawa fill up fast on weekend nights, so reserve at least a week in advance.
Carry cash — stalls at the floating market, the railway market, and many old sweet shops still mainly take cash.
Bring comfortable walking shoes — both Khao Wang and Khao Luang Cave involve climbing up and down, and some surfaces are slippery.
Watch out for monkeys — both Khao Wang and Khao Luang Cave have plenty of them, so keep food and valuables well out of reach.

faq.q: Can you do Samut Songkhram and Phetchaburi in 3 days?
faq.a: Easily — the two provinces are on the same road, and driving from Amphawa down to Phetchaburi takes only about 40–50 minutes. This plan keeps you in Samut Songkhram for the first two days for the railway market, the floating market, and the fireflies, then crosses into old-town Phetchaburi on day three before you head home. No rushing and no backtracking.

faq.q: Which days should I go to see everything?
faq.a: Leaving on a Friday is best, because Amphawa Floating Market only opens Friday to Sunday, roughly 11:00–20:00, and those are the nights you can ride out to see the fireflies. The Maeklong Railway Market and Phetchaburi's sights are open every day, so a Friday-to-Sunday trip lets you catch it all.

faq.q: How far is it from Amphawa to Phetchaburi, and how do you get there?
faq.a: Not far — about 45 kilometres along Highway 4 (Phetkasem), under an hour by car. If you don't have your own car, there are regular Maeklong–Phetchaburi vans, but spots like Khao Luang Cave and Bang Kung Camp are far more convenient with a car.

faq.q: Where should you go in Phetchaburi if you only have one day?
faq.a: The main stop is Phra Nakhon Khiri, or Khao Wang — head up to see the Rama IV palace and the town view — followed by Wat Mahathat Worawihan with its five-spired prang in the centre of town, Wat Yai Suwannaram with its Phetchaburi craftsmanship, and Khao Luang Cave where light filters down onto the Buddha images. Finish by buying custard cake to take home.

faq.q: Which shop should I buy Phetchaburi custard cake from?
faq.a: The well-known old-name shops are Mae Kim Lai and Mae Kim Lang, run by siblings who've been selling it for decades. They have several branches, both in town and along the Bangkok-bound side of Phetkasem Road, so it's easy to stop by on the drive back. Besides custard cake, they have plenty of other Phetchaburi sweets to choose from too.
